transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-19
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO - Atlas Health), Tom Alvarez (Lead ML Eng), Sara Khan (Security)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account, and with Priya who's our product SE. Maya and team, thanks for taking the time. Quick check-in, is this still a 45-ish minute walkthrough?
[00:08] Maya: Yep that's right, thanks Jordan. We mainly want to see the console tracing, how error analysis and request logs look, and how we'd debug production spikes. Also Sara will ask a few security questions.
[00:17] Jordan: Perfect. Priya, you want to kick us off in the console?
[00:20] Priya: Yeah sure. I'm sharing my screen now. Let me know if you can't see.
[00:25] [screen share sounds, slight delay]
[00:28] Priya: Ok, so this is the Redwood Console -> Observability -> Traces view. You can pivot by route, model, and timeframe. Here I've filtered to the chat endpoint that most of our demo traffic uses. First thing you see is a latency histogram, then the trace span waterfall.
[00:45] Tom: Looks clean. How often do you sample traces?
[00:49] Priya: Default is adaptive sampling — high error-rate flows get sampled more aggressively. For POCs we can increase sample rate or do full capture for a short window. Sampling settings are per-tenant.
[01:02] Sara: And those traces include request payloads? We need to make sure PHI is not stored in logs.
[01:08] Priya: Good call. By default we redaction PII/PHI and we have toggles — we can show schema-only, or full payload if you opt-in. For customers concerned about retention we support short retention windows and also KMS-backed encryption for logs at rest.
[01:22] Maya: Can you show an error analysis example? Recently we had spikes where tokenization errors or model timeouts happened.
[01:30] Priya: Yep. I'm switching to Error Analysis. Here you can group errors by type, route, model version, and metadata like tenant id or user id. This example shows a spike last Thursday — most were 504 gateway timeouts when sequence lengths spiked. You can click into a cluster and it surfaces representative traces and request logs.
[01:52] [00:01:54] Jordan: There's a quick note — our "KV cache" sometimes is transcribed as K-V cash in some of our docs, ignore that, it's the same thing.
[02:02] Tom: When you say representative traces, are those full spans with kernel timings? We need to correlate with our batcher metrics.
[02:10] Priya: Yes you get span timings such as queue wait, tokenize, kv-lookup, attention, kernel-exec. Those align with the runtime metrics. If you push your batcher metrics via our endpoint we can correlate them side-by-side.
[02:24] Tom: Nice. Can we export raw request logs? Our infra team wants the raw JSON of the requests for deeper analysis.
[02:29] Priya: Absolutely. Request Logs tab — you can export as gzipped JSON or stream via our S3 export integration. We also have a request-logs API for real-time streaming to a customer-owned bucket.
[02:41] Sara: About S3 export — is that within our VPC or do you push out? Data residency is important.
[02:47] Jordan: For Private deployments we can run in your VPC or on-prem. For hosted, data export goes to a customer-owned bucket in your cloud account via a push mechanism. We'll share the architecture diagram and the S3 IAM policy.
[02:59] Maya: On the hosted side, what's the retention? We typically need 30-90 days of logs for audits.
[03:05] Priya: Hosted default is 30 days, configurable up to 365 for an add-on. Private can match any retention you need as it's customer-controlled.
[03:13] Tom: Quick question on request ids — if we provide a list of failing requestIDs, can you lookup the full trace and console jump-to?
[03:20] Priya: Yep, paste them into the lookup box and the console will jump you directly to the trace plus request log and associated model variant.
[03:27] Tom: Sweet. We'll send a list after this call.
[03:30] [03:31] Maya: Could you demo a debugging flow — like from an alert to root cause and fix?
[03:36] Priya: Sure. I'm going to simulate an alert for increased error rate. So alert fires, you get an entry in the incidents panel. Click "Investigate" and it opens the correlated traces and the top error clusters. From there you can do a diff across model versions and route configs. I'll filter to the failing route.
[04:00] Priya: You can also attach a reproduction prompt and run a canned eval — we capture the exact model input, model variant, and kernel profile so you can reproduce locally if you pull the same model artifact.
[04:15] Tom: How does the console handle automatic fallbacks? We sometimes prefer fallback to a smaller model during overloads.
[04:20] Priya: Rollout policies support automatic fallback to a compatible model variant by policy. You can set thresholds e.g., latency > 800ms triggers fallback to the gpt-small variant. All fallbacks are recorded in the trace metadata.
[04:33] Sara: For compliance, we need audit logs for admin actions — who flipped what rollout, who accessed logs. Is that surfaced?
[04:40] Jordan: Yes, we have an audit log view with SSO/SAML identities mapped to actions. Logs can be exported to your SIEM and are retained per your retention policy.
[04:49] Maya: Any known gaps with SOC2? We need the cert and the control matrix.
[04:54] Jordan: We'll send our SOC2 report and the control matrix after the call. Also our KMS integration details and HSM options for Private. Link in the follow-up: https://redwood.ai/security (note: placeholder).
[05:05] [05:06] Tom: Ok, now the more gnarly case: we had a recent problem where long sequences caused sudden memory pressure and subsequent 503s. Can Redwood traces show memory pressure or GPU OOM spans?
[05:18] Priya: The runtime emits metrics — OOMs, memory high-water, kernel errors — those are included as span-level events. We also surface per-token kernel latency which often shows the hotspot before OOM. For private deployments you can stream GPU metrics into the console and correlate.
[05:33] Tom: Would you need agents installed on our infra for the private case?
[05:36] Jordan: No agents; runtime sidecars collect metrics and push to the control plane over the private link or within your VPC. For on-prem we have a connector that runs as a lightweight process.
[05:46] Maya: Can we do a quick live lookup? I'll paste a sample requestID I grabbed earlier.
[05:50] Tom: I just uploaded a small CSV with three failing IDs to the shared drive, link in chat.
[05:55] Priya: Found it. Pasting the id into the console now... pulling trace... here we go. You can see the waterfall: queue wait was small, then tokenize spiked, then kv-lookup took longer, then a kernel-exec which timed out. Representative request shows input document had a 32k token doc because of a bad ingestion chunker.
[06:18] Maya: Great, that's exactly the pattern we saw. So fix is to enforce chunking at ingestion or increase the max seq in model config?
[06:26] Priya: Both are options. Usually we recommend enforcing chunking, and also configure a soft limit with a graceful reject so user-facing errors are friendlier. If you want to support longer sequences, you can use a different model variant or change runtime memory config in a Private deployment.
[06:41] Sara: Are there alerts we can configure for tokenization anomalies?
[06:45] Priya: Yes, anomaly detectors — you can alert on token distribution, unexpected sequence lengths, or KV cache miss rates. Alerts integrate with PagerDuty/Slack/email.
[06:53] Jordan: Quick clarification — our Console labels sometimes say "request logs" but the internal name is request-events, occasionally transcribed as request-lodges in older docs, but it's the same tab.
[07:03] [07:04] Maya: Good to know.
[07:06] Tom: About integrations — can we pull the raw traces into Datadog or Grafana?
[07:10] Priya: We have exporters: Datadog, Prometheus, and an HTTP webhook for custom sinks. For Grafana you can query the metrics backend directly if you're on a Private deployment.
[07:21] Tom: One more thing — for the POC we'd like to run a traffic replay of a 2-hour window. How does Redwood handle replay and caching?
[07:29] Priya: We support replay with preserved request IDs and allow you to enable/disable KV cache during replay. For performance testing we can run a replay in a sandbox tenant and capture traces. If you want to avoid incurring model inference costs we also support dry-run mode which simulates latency profiles.
[07:45] Maya: Cost is a factor. Can you give a rough unit-cost delta between hosted and Dedicated?
[07:51] Jordan: Short answer: hosted is simpler and often cheaper for low volume; Dedicated reduces per-token cost at scale and gives committed throughput. I'll send a tailored pricing sheet after we get your traffic profile.
[08:02] Sara: For encryption — do you support customer-managed keys for logs and model artifacts?
[08:07] Priya: Yes, KMS support for hosted and Private. For on-prem we can integrate with your HSM. All keys and integrations are documented.
[08:15] Maya: Ok this has been very useful. Any limitations we should know about?
[08:19] Priya: A couple notes: streaming traces for extremely high QPS might be sampled, and exporting huge volumes of raw request logs is best done via S3 streaming. Also some older model variants don't emit all kernel-level spans — newer runtimes are richer. We'll flag those in the docs.
[08:35] Tom: Sounds fair.
[08:38] Jordan: Next steps quick recap: we'll send SOC2 + security pack, Priya will provision demo tenant and upload instructions, Tom will send failing request IDs and a sample traffic profile, and we'll schedule a POC kickoff next week.
[08:52] Maya: Works for us. Thanks Jordan and Priya.
[08:55] Sara: Thanks everyone.
[08:57] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up with links and the pricing sheet.
[09:00] [call ends]
